questions.q: What materialization have the staging and intermediate models used so far in this chapter?
options: `view` for staging, `table` for the intermediate model — the defaults
`incremental` for every model built so far
`ephemeral` for every model
None — they haven't been materialized at all yet
questions.explain: Lessons 2-4 used the cheap view default for staging and the table default for the intermediate model — the right choice for those models.

questions.q: What exactly breaks if the final orders fact model stays `table`-materialized indefinitely?
options: Cost and run time grow steadily as history grows — not correctness
The numbers become wrong after a year of data
dbt refuses to run a table model past a certain row count
Power BI can no longer connect to a table-materialized model
questions.explain: A table-materialized model stays correct — it just re-scans and re-derives growing history on every run, which steadily costs more time and compute.

questions.q: Why does the orders fact model hit this problem specifically, versus a one-time seed load?
options: raw_orders gets new rows every day the shop is open, so the full history being re-scanned keeps growing
It's a bigger file size on disk from the start
It's the only model that uses a left join
It uses a different database than the rest of the project
questions.explain: The daily-growing nature of raw_orders, established back in Lesson 1, is exactly why this model's full-rebuild cost keeps climbing.

questions.q: Why does the incremental decision belong on the final fact model rather than Lesson 4's intermediate model?
options: The fact model is the one Finance and Ops's BI reports hit directly and repeatedly — that's the expensive layer to optimize
dbt doesn't allow incremental materialization on intermediate models
The intermediate model has no columns that could serve as a watermark
It doesn't matter which model gets the incremental logic
questions.explain: Putting the incremental logic on the wrong layer would solve the wrong model's cost problem — the fact model is the one repeatedly queried.

questions.q: What's the real reason an incremental model ends up faster than a table model on a growing source?
options: It skips re-deriving rows that were already correctly built in a previous run
It uses a smaller amount of disk space for the same data
It compiles to a completely different query language
It automatically indexes every column
questions.explain: The speed gain comes specifically from not reprocessing history that's already correct — only new/changed rows get processed each run.
